To highlight how global matching models can produce memorability effects, we conducted simulations using the REM (Retrieving Effectively from Memory) model framework (Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997), which represents items as arbitrary vectors of feature values drawn from a geometric distribution, such that some feature values are more common than others. This model has been widely applied and found to explain core phenomena in recognition memory (Malmberg et al., 2019; Mohamed et al., 2026). However, while numerous global matching models share the foundational principle that summed similarity (the aggregated similarity between a probe item and all stored memory traces) plays a central role in recognition decisions (e.g., Clark & Gronlund, 1996; Nosofsky, 1988; Osth & Dennis, 2024), we focus on REM because it implements this principle through an elegant Bayesian likelihood ratio framework, making it ideal for examining how apparent memorability effects emerge from relational distinctiveness. Our core results also hold in other global matching models that give rare features extra weight, like a hybrid-similarity exemplar model (Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003; see SI Appendix, Section 3).

In particular, in judging whether an item is "old" or "new", REM uses what amounts to counterfactual Bayesian reasoning: it computes the likelihood that an observed memory match signal would occur if the item had been studied versus if it had not. Consider a person with a distinctive face tattoo. When a tattooed face is studied, the same face on a later recognition test may produce an exceptionally strong memory match signal not because it matches its memory representation better than an average face without a tattoo would, but because the tattoo is rare and therefore greatly reduces the probability of a similar match signal arising from a face that was not studied. In terms of the likelihood ratio, the rare feature primarily affects the denominator, since the probability of such a match under the alternative hypothesis that the face was not studied is very small. Therefore, when a match occurs along this rare dimension, it constitutes exceptionally strong evidence that this particular person was studied. However, this is not intrinsic memorability, because it is always a ratio that depends fundamentally on the lures, not just the shown item. Thus, any other face with the same kind of tattoo will also generate strong 'old' evidence and thus many false alarms, as we find in our face experiment below. In contrast, an average person without distinctive features may actually be more similar to other studied faces (e.g., have a higher summed similarity to the memory set), yet produce a weaker recognition signal because many unstudied faces also share these common features, making them not very diagnostic of a true match.

Simulations of Memorability as an Emergent Property

We generated simulated data that had the same approximate structure as the most well understood memorability dataset (Kramer et al., 2023), which provides memorability scores for the images and features of the THINGS image set (Hebart et al., 2019). Hebart et al. (2020) showed that human similarity judgments for this image set were well captured by a sparse set of 49 distinct visual/semantic features. We therefore generated a set of 1,600 simulated items (the size of the image sets in our behavioral experiments), each represented by a vector of 49 feature values to match these human data in approximate structure. In our simulation, the 49 feature values for each item were generated randomly and independently from a geometric distribution (see Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997), and thus have no particular meaning and no intrinsic relationship to memorability. Items were then "shown" to the model, and episodic memory encoding followed the standard REM procedure (SI Appendix, Section 1). To mimic the structure of typical memorability experiments as well as our subsequent behavioral experiments, we designed the study and test items to be random subsets of this simulated image set. In particular, mimicking our behavioral experiments, we conducted 10,000 independent recognition memory experiment simulations, each involving a simulated participant studying a random draw of 40 items and then being tested on 40 items: 20 of the studied items (old) intermixed with 20 additional items drawn from the 1,600-item set that were not studied in that simulation (new lures).

For each simulated recognition test, we compute the hit rate (calling an item old when it was old) for each item and the false alarm rate (calling an item old when it was new) for that same item across the 10,000 simulation runs. Accurate measures of memorability would require ROC analysis (e.g., Brady et al., 2023). However, for comparison to the existing memorability literature, we focus here on hit rate and/or corrected recognition rate (hits minus false alarms).

All of our analyses are robust to using d′ or d a (SI Appendix, Sections 1 and 2). We find that some items are consistently more memorable than others across "participants" (Fig. 1a), mimicking apparent intrinsic memorability. However, in this simulation all features are randomly generated and contain no actual semantic or visual information that could make them intrinsically memorable. Thus, this memorability could not be predicted by anything intrinsic about the features themselves, but instead was strongly predicted by each item's distinctiveness in the overall image set (i.e., how dissimilar it was to other items in the image set). As noted above, many specific aspects of the distinctiveness of an item and its features play a role in REM's decision via the likelihood ratio. However, in line with the general structure of global matching models, we found items that are more similar to other items in aggregate (summed similarity of raw feature representations, not differentiating by rare vs. common features as REM does) have greater interference in matching and thus worse memory performance (memorability vs. summed similarity to all other items across all of the features: r = -0.56, 95% CI [-0.59, -0.52], p < 0.01; Fig. 1a). As described in the supplement, the breakdown of this effect into hits vs. false alarms depends on the nature of the crowding in the stimulus set and the way the model weights rarity vs. summed similarity (SI Appendix, Section 4).

A core conclusion of the memorability literature has been that not only do images vary in memorability, but this image-level variance is predictable based on the features of the images (Kramer et al., 2023). For example, of the 49 visual and semantic features, some predict better memorability (e.g., body part-relatedness) and some worse memorability (e.g., electronics). Does the same occur here, where features are arbitrary and such relationships could not be intrinsic? In our simulations, individual features also show reliable correlations with memorability (Fig. 1b). Crucially, however, each feature's correlation with memorability was predicted by how much that feature correlated with overall item similarity, not by anything intrinsic to the features (as nothing could be intrinsic here, with arbitrary features: ρ = -0.44, 95% CI [-0.70, -0.30], p < 0.01; Fig. 1b).

Overall, with no intrinsic features that are in any way tied to memorability, REM reproduces the key aspects of the data that are generally argued to provide evidence for intrinsic memorability. This is evidence that such a pattern is not diagnostic of intrinsic memorability, but can arise from the distribution of studied items and lures in an arbitrary stimulus set with a fully relational model, where rarity weights feature matches and summed similarity drives decisions in the same way to both old and new items.

REM also reproduces what has been offered as the strongest evidence for intrinsic memorability, that the rank order of items' memorability is stable across large changes in context (Bylinskii et al., 2015). In a simulation of Bylinskii et al.'s within-category and across-category contexts, items kept their memorability ranks across contexts (Spearman ρ = 0.60, 95% CI [0.56, 0.63]; ρ = 0.60 for hit rates in the human data), because adding many items from the same category raised the summed similarity of every item in that category without actually changing which of them were the most distinctive (ρ = 0.93, 95% CI [0.92, 0.94]; SI Appendix, Section 3). Importantly, these results (and this cross-context consistency) do not appear to depend on the particular settings we chose for the simulations. They held across a wide range of REM's parameters and decision criteria, in continuous recognition as well as study-test lists, and when the simulated items were given the measured features of THINGS concepts rather than randomly generated ones as well as in a hybrid-similarity exemplar model (Nosofsky et al., 2025; SI Appendix, Section 3).

Direct Manipulations: Changing What an Item Is Studied or Tested With

Because global matching models have been a dominant theoretical framework in recognition memory for decades, supported by a large body of empirical evidence, we suggest that the burden of proof shifts to the intrinsic memorability account: what positive evidence supports it? While we cannot prove intrinsic memorability does not exist, we can test a set of predictions that is unique to global matching models, namely that explicitly manipulating similarity structure should change what appears memorable and that memorability in existing image sets should follow the similarity structure of the items studied and tested.

Inverting Memorability Through Direct Manipulation of Distinctiveness at Study

Our first behavioral experiment directly tests whether the predictions of global matching models generalize from simulations to human memory by attempting to invert memorability rankings through systematic manipulation of study context, with test context held fixed. Notably, we manipulate context in a way that does not just shift all items upward and downward in terms of their overall similarity to other items studied (as in Bylinskii et al., 2015, which is not diagnostic of emergent vs. intrinsic memorability, as shown by the simulation), but instead differentially shifts distinctiveness across items.

In each study/test block, we selected five critical items from the THINGS image set spanning the full memorability range based on Kramer et al.'s (2023) scores, one item each from the lowest 20%, 20-40%, 40-60%, 60-80%, and highest 20% memorability bins. We then constructed the similarity context around each critical item. Originally highly memorable items were surrounded in the study list by many similar items from the image set (8 similar items, with 4, 2 and 1 for the intermediate bins; SI Appendix, Section 1), reducing their distinctiveness in the list context. Conversely, originally poorly memorable items were placed in lists with few or no similar items (0 similar items), making them the most distinctive items in their list context. This approach directly manipulates the relational property of distinctiveness while keeping the intrinsic properties of the items themselves unchanged.

Consistent with our emergent account, when comparing the original memorability scores of the items from Kramer et al. (2023) against the memorability in this task, we found a significant inversion (ρ = -0.50, 95% CI [-0.76, -0.18], p < 0.01; see Fig. 1c). This suggests that the distinctiveness was a better predictor of item memorability than intrinsic properties of the images.

Inverting Memorability Through Direct Manipulation of Distinctiveness at Test

The inversion experiment changed what each item was studied alongside without changing the test structure. However, global matching models also predict that what an item is tested against should be key to its memorability. Our second experiment tests this prediction with faces, focusing on a version of the tattoo example above. In particular, we held the studied faces fixed and changed only whether a new face at test contained the same rare feature.

Participants studied 50 faces (N = 100, preregistered; SI Appendix, Section 5).

Six of the 50 studied faces had a feature that is rare in everyday life (e.g., an electricgreen mohawk). Each rare feature was present on two different people. One of them was studied, and the other could sometimes appear at test as a lure with the same rare feature. The rest of the test was ordinary faces, half of them studied and half new. If a rare feature makes a face intrinsically memorable, a studied rare face should be easy to tell apart from any new face.

If memorability is relational, the rare feature should help only when no new face at test also has it.

Studied faces with a rare feature were called old on 90% of trials, compared with 80% for ordinary studied faces (t(99) = 5.29, p < 0.001). Unrelated new faces, which had no rare feature, were called old on only 41% of trials. Against these new faces, rare faces were much more discriminable than ordinary faces (d a = 1.67 vs. 1.00; Fig. 1d, red line). However, the new face with the same rare feature was called old on 59% of trials (0.18 more often than an unrelated new face, 95% CI [0.12, 0.24], t(99) = 5.89, p < 0.001). The rare feature thus raised false alarms even more than it raised hits (by 0.07, 95% CI [0.01, 0.14], t(99) = 2.17, p = 0.033).

Against this lure, the same rare faces were no more discriminable than an ordinary face (d a = 1.00, 95% CI [0.75, 1.25]; Fig. 1d, blue dashed line). Comparing each face against itself across participants, the rare faces were also no more memorable than ordinary faces (hit rate minus false alarm rate 0.33 vs. 0.38), because their extra hits were matched by extra false alarms (SI Appendix, Section 5).

Thus, a rare feature of the kind usually thought to make a face memorable did not make that face intrinsically more memorable. Matching on the rare feature was strong evidence that a face was studied, whether or not the rest of the face matched, rather than providing any facespecific advantage.

Overall, both of our targeted experiments changed the context an item was judged in while holding the item itself constant. The first changed how many similar items were studied alongside the item, and the second whether a similar item appeared at test. If memorability were intrinsic, neither manipulation should matter, since the images and the faces were the same in every condition. Global matching models predict both effects we observed, in particular a cost to similarity in both situations in terms of the ability to discriminate old from new items. Thus, we suggest, in line with decades of work on recognition memory, that a memorability score is necessarily a claim about both an item and the set it was measured in.

Representational Analyses: Memorability Follows the Structure of the Image Set

We next turn to memorability in large-scale image sets, the primary domain that has been the focus of the intrinsic memorability literature. To understand real-world memorability in this context, where similarity is not explicitly manipulated (or simulated), we must specify the representational space within which distinctiveness operates in human memory. Before any particular memory episode occurs, perception and cognition have already structured the world into a particular representational format. Episodic memory operates on top of this pre-existing structure, such that when we encode a particular image or event, the memory representation inherits the structure and biases of the underlying perceptual and semantic space (e.g., Nagy et al., 2025). This raises a key question for understanding human memorability in real image sets: what are the "features" that determine distinctiveness in human cognition? Clearly people represent some aspects of the environment more than others (e.g., faces more than blades of grass), and this will shape their representations and thus memory confusions. This shaping is evident in the representational space of the THINGS image set (the dominant image set used to study memorability). The similarity structure of this image set, as captured by the 49dimensional feature embedding that explains human similarity judgments (Hebart et al., 2020), devotes substantial representational capacity to features related to animacy (body parts, animals, insects) because human cognition allocates disproportionate neural and attentional resources to animate things, given their ecological and social importance (Nairne et al., 2017).

How will this impact memory? Consider the 49-dimensional THINGS representational space. If an image set contains many animate items, such that animate items are common on individual study lists and as test lures, they will occupy densely packed regions of representational space, making individual animate items less distinctive and therefore less memorable. Conversely, if animate items are rare in an image set and therefore rare on individual study lists and test sets, they become highly distinctive within that context. Thus, the apparent "intrinsic memorability" of animate items in standard image sets need not reflect animacy itself, nor the extra representational capacity devoted to those features, but the fact that animate items are relatively sparse in the image set despite falling in a region of representational space to which humans devote substantial resources. Although humans clearly represent more and richer features about some stimuli than others, this does not allow one to make any prediction about memorability per se without also taking into account the over-or underrepresentation of items in the image set, and thus the study and test sets, relative to this representational space.

To test the emergent memorability account, we used the THINGS image set to construct three complementary representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs), operationalizing how similar vs. dissimilar items were in this representational space in order to allow us to examine the degree of over-vs. underrepresentation and what it predicts about memory performance.

One similarity structure was derived from the 49-dimensional feature embeddings known to capture human similarity judgments (Hebart et al., 2020). A second was based on macaque IT cortex neural activity patterns (Papale et al., 2025), serving as a biological model of object representation. Both these 49-dimensional features and IT patterns are at the concept/category level, not the image level. Thus, where required to get individual image predictions, we also use a third similarity structure, an RDM based on pooled computer vision models (ResNet18, VGG16, AlexNet, and CLIP), though given this is unlikely to be well aligned with humans (see Simpson et al., 2026) we use human and monkey data where possible. Note that these

The Similarity Structure of an Image Set Determines What Will Be Memorable

As noted, the targeted inversion and face experiments differ from conventional memorability paradigms in a crucial way, in that we deliberately constructed the similarity context, at study in the first and at test in the second, rather than randomly sampling from a large image set. We did this in order to show directly that memory performance depends crucially on both of these factors and cannot be understood without considering which other items are present at study and test. Standard memorability studies instead sample items at random from large image sets, in order to average over many similarity contexts (e.g., Isola et al., 2014; Kramer et al., 2023). If our distinctiveness account is correct, however, then random sampling cannot eliminate these effects. Instead, the similarity structure of the image set itself should determine which items appear memorable, even when items are randomly sampled for individual experiments, because sampling from the image sets determines the average context at study and test. Study context is straightforward to see, but test context is also likely critical to why image sets affect memorability (e.g., in THINGS, an image of a face is, on average, much less similar to the lures it is tested against than an image of a chainsaw is). This is the dependence on lures that we isolated in our face experiment (Fig. 1d), except that in a standard memorability study the image set, rather than the experimenter, decides how often the lures share an item's features.

By measuring distinctiveness in similarity spaces derived from human judgments and from neural data, we next assess whether putatively intrinsically memorable items stand out from their context along dimensions that are psychologically and biologically meaningful in previous memorability data, as global matching models predict. To test this, we reanalyzed the Kramer et al. (2023) memorability findings, asking how the structure of the image set predicts which 'features' predict item memorability. We focus on Kramer et al. (2023) because their work provides in many ways the strongest and most interpretable evidence for the intrinsic memorability account. They show how the 49 features derived from human similarity data in the THINGS image set (Hebart et al., 2020) relate to memorability. They find, for example, that images high on the body-part related feature are among the best remembered by participants, whereas items that score high on the electronics/technology feature tend to be poorly remembered by participants. This feature-level analysis offers both greater statistical power and greater interpretability than item-level memorability scores alone: rather than asking whether a particular image happens to be well-remembered with no clear explanation for why, they ask which psychological dimensions systematically predict memorability. We can therefore straightforwardly ask whether those dimensions are also ones that track distinctiveness within the structure of the image set.

The feature-based analysis is also likely to be more straightforward at the concept level than at the image level. Any noise in the representations we assume for items, or systematic deviations in these representations from actual human representations, will necessarily reduce the ability of a distinctiveness-based account to explain real memorability data (Simpson et al., 2026). However, the greater reliability of measures at the feature level provides a stronger test of how much can be explained by distinctiveness, alleviating this concern to a significant extent.

Reanalyses of Existing Memorability Datasets in Terms of Summed Similarity

In agreement with Kramer et al., we find that individual features out of the 49 visual and semantic features isolated by Hebart et al. (2020) show reliable correlations with memorability (Fig. 2a). However, we also find that the features most predictive of memorability are those that, in the THINGS image set, are most related to distinctiveness, as the emergent memorability view strongly predicts and the intrinsic memorability view gives no reason to expect. In particular, the extent to which features predict memorability is strongly related to the extent to which those features predict overcrowding in the image set (summed similarity vs. memorability: r = -0.612, 95% CI [-0.677, -0.505], p < 0.001; Fig. 2a). Measured with d′, the relationship holds whether crowding is computed over the nearest concepts or over the whole image set, and crowded concepts draw more false alarms at every scale (SI Appendix, Section 4). Similarly, using activity along the monkey multi-unit array as our features (see SI Appendix, Section 1 for further details), we find that features that predict human memorability also predict summed similarity in the neural representations (r = -0.296, 95% CI [-0.389, -0.176], p < 0.001), although naturally these measures are less reliable and less aligned with human representations. In other words, "body-part related" predicts memorability, as Kramer et al. showed. However, it is also one of the best predictors of low summed similarity to other items in the THINGS image set, making such items on average unique at study and at test, a highly diagnostic prediction unique to emergent memorability theories that intrinsic accounts have no reason to expect. This relationship does not appear to be specific to the published embedding or to object images. Summed similarity computed from the features of deep networks also predicts memorability in the most well studied dataset of face memorability (Bainbridge et al., 2013) and a core dataset on scene memorability (Isola et al., 2011), with this summed similarity measure predicting about two thirds of the maximum possible correlation with memorability in these datasets despite the intrinsic memorability account having no reason to expect any relationship to summed similarity at all (SI Appendix, Section 6). Similarly, we note that Atzert et al. (2025 Atzert et al. ( , 2026) ) recently reported that scene images that are less typical of their category are better remembered, and argue that scene memorability reflects representational distinctiveness within visual categories.

The trial-level data of Kramer et al. (2023) allow a direct test of whether random sampling removes the effect of context, since each participant saw a different stream of images.

While this continuous recognition paradigm does not allow careful isolation of study and test, or computation of more accurate memory measures (SI Appendix, Section 2), we nonetheless find that the same image was remembered less well when the images that preceded it in a participant's stream were more similar to it, regardless of whether similarity was measured from human judgments or in a purely visual space derived from deep networks (SI Appendix, Section 7). When we ranked each image's trials by how similar the preceding stream was, d′ fell by 0.51 (95% CI [0.48, 0.54]) from the least to the most similar context, 1.34 times the standard deviation of d′ across images (SI Appendix, Fig. S15a). When we ran Kramer et al.'s own test for context (which they argued contributed minimally) on the same trials, it left the image rankings intact, because as in our REM simulations, splitting participants by how many exemplars of a category they saw shifts the competitors of every image in that category at once (SI Appendix, Fig. S16) and thus masks the role of context.

Thus, the mismatch between how densely THINGS samples a region of representational space and how much of that space people devote to it (e.g., few animate concepts but many electronics) leads features like body parts to appear intrinsically memorable when they may owe their memorability to being underrepresented in the image set relative to the richness with which humans process and represent them.

Image Set Manipulation Experiments

We next consider a key causal prediction of the emergent memorability account with respect to this image set argument. If we systematically change the similarity structure of an image set, features that were originally "intrinsically memorable" should lose their memorability advantage, while a new set of features should emerge as apparently memorable. This prediction directly contradicts purely intrinsic views of memorability, which predict that features maintain their memorability regardless of the makeup of the image set that is used to test memorability. To directly test whether memorability is a consequence of similarity structure rather than an intrinsic property of images, we subsampled the THINGS image set into two image sets of 1,600 images each, with contrasting representational distributions (Fig. 2b and c). Throughout, the similarity space is fixed, insofar as each concept has the same coordinates in the 49dimensional embedding in both image sets and in every model and analysis. The sets differ only in which concepts are sampled, and therefore in how crowded each concept's neighborhood is at study and test. The first (the maintained image set) preserved the original similarity structure of the full image set. The second (the changed image set) sampled the same space differently, partially inverting which regions were crowded (to the degree possible), so that concepts previously occupying crowded and overrepresented regions of feature space now became relatively distinct. It was not possible to fully invert the similarity structure because of the discrete nature of the image set, e.g., only so many animate items were available when subsampling the THINGS image set. Nonetheless, the changed image set switched the relative prevalence of different features in the image set, and thus changed the similarity structure with respect to the Hebart et al. (2020) features. Because the lures were drawn from the same image set as the study lists, this also changed which features were distinctive relative to the lures (e.g., the changed set oversampled concepts high on features that had predicted good memory in THINGS, so that these concepts now met many close competitors at test).

If memorability were intrinsic to images, the same features should predict memory performance regardless of which image set a given image appears in. Instead, in a recognition memory experiment with these stimuli (SI Appendix, Section 1), we found the opposite. The relationships between features and memorability in the maintained image set closely replicated those of the full THINGS image set (r = 0.84, 95% CI [0.79, 0.86], p < 0.001; Fig. 2d), and distinctiveness in this image set predicted memorability, using both human and monkey similarity spaces to measure distinctiveness (r = -0.89, 95% CI [-0.91, -0.85], and r = -0.63, 95% CI [-0.68, -0.53], respectively; both p < 0.001). When similarity structure was changed, however, the same features that had previously predicted good memory now predicted poor memory (r = -0.33, 95% CI [-0.43, -0.21], p < 0.001), with a new set of features becoming memorable. The particular features that were now memorable were again predicted by their distinctiveness in both human (r = -0.75, 95% CI [-0.81, -0.64], p < 0.001) and monkey (r = -0.45, 95% CI [-0.51, -0.36], p < 0.001) similarity spaces, even though they were different features compared to the maintained image set. These results show that which features are memorable is not fixed but depends on the context in which images are encountered, which is determined by the image set that lists are sampled from. In addition, when we gave a global matching model the same study lists and test trials that our participants saw, it reproduced the inversion of Fig. 1c and correctly predicted that an image would be better remembered in the image set where it was more distinctive (SI Appendix, Section 8). The observed change in memory for the same image between sets came mostly from false alarms, that is, from how often participants called the image old when it was a lure (SI Appendix, Section 8). The relationship between summed similarity and memorability, at the level of both concepts and features, also did not depend on our participant exclusion criteria (SI Appendix, Section 1).

Reducing Variability in Distinctiveness Reduces Variability in Memorability

Some proponents of intrinsic memorability acknowledge that extrinsic effects (like overloading with similar items, as in the changed image set) may impact memorability in addition to intrinsic effects (e.g., Bylinskii et al., 2015). In theory, then, intrinsic memorability could still exist, with all of our reported effects being extrinsic memorability effects that ride on top of these intrinsic effects. Notably, there is no positive evidence for this, as we have shown so far that the full set of results typically taken to reflect intrinsic memorability can easily arise in simpler models that have no such concept, and tested direct causal predictions of our emergent account. However, we reasoned that if memorability variation arises largely from distinctiveness variation, then sampling as uniformly from representational space as possible should reduce variability in distinctiveness and diminish the variability typically observed in how different features relate to memorability, without any overloading of similar items (in the resulting image set, no category made up more than about 13% of the concepts). Because the lures are drawn from the same image set, such sampling should also reduce the variability in how distinctive features are, on average, relative to the lures, and so weaken how strongly any given feature predicts memorability.

By contrast, if memorability were intrinsic, visual features should predict memorability as strongly in such an image set as in the original and maintained image sets above.

In building this new image set, we were able to reduce summed similarity variation: whereas the maintained image set showed broad variability in summed similarity across concepts (Mean = 0.18, SD = 0.00322), reflecting the uneven crowding of representational space that characterizes the THINGS image set, the reduced variability image set showed a sharply peaked distribution around the same mean (SD = 0.00156), confirming that differences in distinctiveness had been successfully reduced (Fig. 2b and SI Appendix, Fig. S1). This almost certainly overstates how far we equalized true distinctiveness (e.g., we equated concepts rather than individual images, and the 49 features capture only some of the dimensions along which people confuse items), which will necessarily attenuate any reduction in the correlations between features and memorability. Nonetheless, consistent with our emergent memorability account, this attempted equalization of distinctiveness substantially reduced the ability of image features to predict memorability. Across all 49 features, the summed squared correlation with corrected recognition dropped by 27% relative to the maintained image set (one-sided bootstrap p = 0.036; Fig. 2h).

Because the two image sets share only some of their concepts, we also repeated this analysis, as a more powerful test, on the 559 concepts that appear in both, holding the concepts and their features fixed. On these concepts, the summed squared correlation dropped by 34% across 10,000 participant resamples (95% CI [4%, 57%], two-sided bootstrap p = 0.032). Memorability also varied reliably less across concepts in the reduced set. On the shared concepts, the reliability-corrected variance of concept memorability (the covariance of concept memorability between random halves of the participants, which trial-to-trial noise does not contribute to) was 38% lower in the reduced set (two-sided permutation p = 0.020, shuffling participants between the two sets). Furthermore, the features that lost the most predictive power were those most tied to distinctiveness in the maintained set (Spearman ρ = 0.56 across the 49 features, p < 0.001; ρ = 0.37, p = 0.008, controlling for each feature's correlation with memorability in the maintained set).

This was true even though the reduced image set does not overload any one category and instead includes each category in study lists and as lures at test in a proportion closer to that implied by people's internal visual and semantic representation. This pattern suggests that the closer an image set gets to being equally spaced in human representational space, the less image features predict memorability.

General Discussion

The present work challenges the view that some images are intrinsically more memorable than others. Drawing on global matching models of recognition memory, we propose that what looks like intrinsic memorability is better understood as an emergent consequence of relational structure, that is, how similar or distinct an item is relative to everything else a person is tasked with remembering on a study list or discriminating it from at test. We formalized this idea using global matching models, showing that distinctiveness within a stimulus set, not any fixed property of individual images, is sufficient to produce the memorability effects documented in the literature. Directly manipulating context changed memorability in the way this account predicts. When memorable images were surrounded by similar items at study, their memorability ranking inverted (ρ = -0.50), and a rare feature made a face more memorable only when no new face at test contained the same feature. Reanalyses of the THINGS image set confirmed that the features that predict human memorability are precisely those that track distinctiveness within the image sets used to study memorability (r = -0.61). Direct manipulations of image set structure showed that the same features can flip from memorable to forgettable depending on the image set images are sampled from. Finally, reducing variation in how well features predict distinctiveness also reduced how well features predicted memorability (by 27%; Fig. 2h). Taken together, these findings suggest that memorability is not a property to be explained at the level of individual images but a relational phenomenon that emerges from how distinct items are in visual and conceptual similarity.

Memorability as Emergent From Relational Processes

Across these approaches, our results show that the methods used to establish intrinsic memorability (e.g., the consistency of memorability scores across participants within stimuli sampled randomly from the same image set or related image sets with the same biases) do not rule out a relational account, because any study that samples from the same image distribution will inherit the same similarity structure. Thus, to establish that memorability is intrinsic rather than relational, one would need to show that images identified as memorable in one context retain that memorability advantage when placed in a context constructed to neutralize their distinctiveness. Our experiments suggest they will not.

Other work has reached related conclusions from quite different directions. For example, Nosofsky et al. (2025) show that a model based on relational similarity structure accounts for a wide range of context-dependent memorability effects in real-world image domains. Their approach relies on fitting a cognitive model directly to individual-item recognition data rather than working at the level of image set structure. Their model makes use of an item-level component (a self-similarity boost for items with salient distinctive features) that plays a role similar to the rare-feature weighting discussed below (see Distinctiveness Relative to the List and to Experience). Similarly, Xie et al. (2020) modeled the memorability of words from their semantic similarity to other words (estimated from co-occurrence statistics), which is also a relational model of why some words are remembered better than others. Other memorability work has addressed context directly, by sampling faces to represent a population or judging each face's distinctiveness on its own (Bainbridge et al., 2013) or by testing whether rankings survive changes in how many exemplars of a category participants saw (Kramer et al., 2023).

However, as noted in our reanalyses of these datasets, these tests ask whether a particular manipulation of list context drives a result rather than whether the structure of the sampled population or lists in general do. In the same THINGS trials in which Kramer et al.'s test leaves rankings intact, we find that the same image is remembered less well after more similar items (SI Appendix, Section 7).

Computational Memorability Models Inadvertently Measure Distinctiveness

We suggest that the logic we apply to behavioral memorability also applies to the enthusiasm surrounding deep learning models of memorability, such as ResMem (Needell & Bainbridge, 2022) and its predecessor MemNet (Khosla et al., 2015). It also applies to neural signatures of memorability identified in the brain, such as memorability-sensitive responses in the medial temporal lobe (Bainbridge et al., 2017) and the magnitude of the IT population response (Jaegle et al., 2019).

The deep learning models achieve impressive prediction accuracy on their training distributions, and this success has been taken as evidence that memorability is a decodable intrinsic visual property. Indeed, recent work has argued that because ResMem makes predictions from a single image with no access to the experimental context, its success demonstrates that it has identified properties intrinsic to the image (Davis & Bainbridge, 2023).

But a model that learns to predict memorability scores from a fixed image distribution will necessarily internalize that distribution's similarity structure (just as language and vision models trained on human-generated data internalize their race and gender biases; Caliskan et al., 2017; Steed & Caliskan, 2021), and these models have no way to distinguish between an image that is memorable because of something fixed about it and an image that is memorable because it happens to be distinctive within the particular image set they were trained on. The lack of access to the experimental context at test time is therefore not the kind of independence from context needed to show that memorability is intrinsic. The training distribution has already supplied the context of what the image is generally surrounded with at study and test. Indeed, consistent with this view of internalized distinctiveness, Jaegle et al. (2019) found that the same correlation between response magnitude and memorability emerges in convolutional neural networks trained only to categorize objects, with no memory objective at all. We suggest the same holds for the brain. A neural "marker" of memorability is, in our account, likely the average difference in response between kinds of stimuli that are under-vs. overrepresented in typical image sets. Animacy, for example, is one of the largest dimensions of response in ventral visual cortex, and animate items are both rare in standard image sets and among the most memorable (Fig. 2a). Any neural measure that distinguishes animate from inanimate stimuli will therefore correlate with memorability across such an image set, even if it contains no information about memory per se. More generally, neural responses to an image shown in isolation can reflect only how that image relates to the observer's past experience, and wherever the images that are rare in an image set also tend to be rare in that experience, correlations between activity and memorability are expected even if memorability is entirely relational. Thus, in an emergent memorability account, the success of both artificial models and biological signatures stems not from uncovering fundamental intrinsic properties of memorability that can be decoded from images independent of context, but instead from internalizing the similarity structure of training data and the distinctiveness of images within that similarity structure into the models and readouts of the brain data.

In line with this prediction, the limitations of models become apparent when tested on novel image sets. Independent benchmarks by Hagen and Espeseth (2023) revealed dramatic performance degradation when ResMem was evaluated across multiple image sets. Variance explained dropped precipitously from approximately 45% on in-distribution data to only 13% on PASCAL-S natural images, 5% on the THINGS object image set, and 2% on object crops, overall representing reductions of 71% to 96% in variance explained in out-of-distribution data.

Distinctiveness Relative to the List and to Experience

An item can be distinctive in two senses, either relative to the other items in the experiment (e.g., it is the only tattooed face on the study list or at test), or relative to what an observer has learned over a lifetime (e.g., face tattoos are rare among the faces people have seen). The first, which we refer to as competitor structure, is what our experiments manipulate, since the items in the experiment determine which stored traces a test item is matched against, and which new items it must be discriminated from. This alone may be sufficient to explain memorability, as the effects of both study and test manipulations are large and easily flip which items are found to be memorable.

However, one specific factor may depend on the lifetime of experience more so than other aspects of memory. That is, in global matching models, the rare-feature weighting (e.g., the greater evidence from a matching green mohawk than from matching brown eyes) can be conceived of in multiple ways, and our data do not distinguish between them. One possibility is that this rare-feature weighting reflects a learned base rate, as typically assumed in REM, where the evidence provided by a match depends on how rare the matching value is in the observer's long-term experience (Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997). Another possibility is that rarity that weights some feature matches more is computed relative to the study list, as in hybrid-similarity exemplar models, where matches on distinctive features add to summed similarity (Knapp et al., 2006; Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003). Our data do not distinguish these, as when we defined rarity only by each participant's own study list, this model reproduced the qualitative patterns in our simulations (SI Appendix, Section 3). A third possibility is that items with common features suffer more interference from memories outside the experiment (i.e., context noise or background noise; Criss & Shiffrin, 2004; Dennis & Humphreys, 2001; Osth & Dennis, 2015). This idea has a long history in face recognition in particular, where typical faces draw more false alarms than unusual ones, possibly because they resemble many faces seen over a lifetime (Bartlett et al., 1984; Vokey & Read, 1992).

Importantly, none of these possibilities amounts to intrinsic memorability. In each, the weight given to a rare feature is computed from an item's relation to other items, whether those are the items on the list or the items an observer has previously encountered, and in each it enters a recognition decision only together with how it relates to each of the items in the experiment, and only in a way that requires consideration of the relation of the feature to the lures. As shown in our face experiment, the diagnosticity of a feature match is not the same thing as the memorability of an item, since what a match on a rare feature is worth depends on whether the lures an item must be distinguished from share that feature.

Overrepresentation of Some Aspects of the World Compared to Experience

We do not deny that humans, on average, represent more useful features about some items (e.g., faces) than others (e.g., individual blades of grass), and thus are typically better at discriminating faces from novel lures than blades of grass. That is, people's representational space is not equally split between all items. However, while memory operates on top of whatever representational structure exists, memory is relational, not intrinsic (just as red is relationally salient, not intrinsically salient). Nothing in our account requires memory representations to reorganize across contexts. In our computational models, the same fixed representational space, applied to a different set of items, produces the changes in memorability we report.

Under a relational account, the fact that humans allocate disproportionate representational resources to animate, social stimuli (e.g., "being alive" explained about half of the explainable variance in similarity judgments of images selected to vary in animacy; Jozwik et al., 2022) does not by itself predict that those stimuli will be more or less memorable. Instead, memorability should depend on whether such stimuli are over-or underrepresented in a given image set relative to their footprint in human representational space. When an image set samples the world in a way that leaves regions of high representational importance sparsely populated, items in those regions become distinctive by default. This appears to be the case for animate and social categories in standard image sets like THINGS (Hebart et al., 2019).

Representational structure clearly shapes the conditions under which distinctiveness arises, but memory depends on distinctiveness, not on representational structure per se.

Apparent category-level, feature-level and item-level differences in memorability likely reflect differences in distinctiveness masquerading as intrinsic properties.

The Importance of Image Sets

Our findings raise important questions about what constitutes appropriate image sets for measuring memory. A practical implication of our emergent memorability account is that there is no such thing as a neutral image set. Every collection of stimuli has a similarity structure that directly shapes which features will appear memorable and which will not. Randomly sampling from an image set does not eliminate this structure but inherits it.

This has concrete consequences for how the field uses large image sets. THINGS was constructed by systematically sampling concrete, picturable nouns from American English. This is a principled procedure (Hebart et al., 2019), but we suggest that it produces a distribution of object concepts that mismatches human representational space in important ways (Contier et al., 2024; see Fig. 2b). The image set contains many more exemplars of categories like tools than of categories like faces, despite the vastly greater importance of social and animate stimuli in human experience and neural representation (Hebart et al., 2020).

What, then, is the ideal image set for measuring memorability? We argue that there is no such image set. The first candidate is a memory list that perfectly equates spacing in human representational space. If items were chosen in proportion to representation, both at study and at test, there would be a lot of things we care about and represent well (e.g., faces) and much less of the things we represent sparsely (e.g., grass blades). Would memorability still exist in this case? On the one hand, a face with a rare feature would still be called old more often in such a list, but this would not be memorability, as it would arise only if the lures were not themselves representative in the same way (since a rare lure is itself called old very frequently if it matches items seen in the list; SI Appendix, Fig. S10b). A second is an image set that matches the frequency of items in the world, which would vastly oversample unimportant stimuli like ants and leaves, which matter little to humans and would therefore be confusable and poorly memorable. And an image set that matches the statistics of human visual experience would still mismatch representation in key ways, devoting far more space to blades of grass and less to large mammals like elephants and zebras than people actually store, leading to unequal memorability for that reason. A key aspect of the emergent memorability account is in fact that no ground truth memorability can exist outside of the context of a particular image set or list.

Measurement and Model Predictions

A final consideration concerns how memory performance should be measured to assess memorability, regardless of whether it is intrinsic or emergent. The most common paradigm in the memorability literature is continuous recognition, in which participants view a long stream of images and respond to each one, typically pressing a key when they detect a repeat (e.g., Bainbridge et al., 2013; Isola et al., 2014). In the present work, rather than continuous recognition, which gives rise to a heavily biased criterion, we used a more standard study-test procedure with confidence ratings, which allows proper ROC analysis. Because we did not have any extreme response biases, we did not find major differences between d a and corrected recognition in our data (see SI Appendix, Section 2), and thus focused on corrected recognition to make our work comparable to previous work in this field. However, this is not a general property of such datasets. Continuous recognition paradigms, which produce few false alarms, generally mix memory with response bias in ways that are difficult to separate (SI Appendix, Section 2).

Our global matching framework also suggests that hits and false alarm rates may be important to analyze separately rather than collapsed into a single measure when considering memorability. The model makes distinct predictions for the two, since items that are typical of a well-represented category (say, a common household object in an image set full of common household objects) will generate not only relatively high hit rates, but also high false alarm rates because novel exemplars of that category will match many stored traces. By contrast, items with rare or unusual features (our face-tattoo example) are predicted to generate high hit rates through a strong self-match likelihood ratio, but may not always lead to high false alarms, as what happens to false alarms depends on the lures.

Conclusion

Over the past two decades, the memorability literature has established that consistency in what people remember is a robust phenomenon. Although intrinsic memorability is, in principle, difficult to falsify, our findings suggest that the methods typically used to support its existence fall short. We have argued that this consistency has been systematically misattributed. Consistency does not require items to have fixed, intrinsic memory properties. It requires only that the distributional structure shaping what is distinctive remains stable across studies, which it does whenever studies draw from the same image sets. Thus, consistency and context-dependence are not in conflict: memorability can be both highly consistent within a given experimental tradition and highly mutable when the similarity structure of the stimulus set changes, as our experiments show.

The relational, emergent account we have advanced is grounded in well-established principles of global matching models that have successfully explained a wide range of memory phenomena for decades. What we have done is apply these principles to the question of memorability, showing that they are sufficient to explain the patterns that have been taken as evidence for something more intrinsic. This does not close the book on memorability research. It simply reframes what the most important questions are. Rather than asking which images are memorable and why, the more productive questions may be: what is the representational structure of the stimulus sets we use, how does that structure shape distinctiveness, how does that depend on study lists vs. test lures, and how can we design experiments that disentangle distributional effects from genuine item-level variation (if such variation exists)? How can we scale up memorability to the real world once we acknowledge the emergent nature of memorability? Answering these questions will require new image sets, new experimental designs, and a closer dialogue between the memorability literature and the broader cognitive science of recognition memory.

Methods

All experiments reported here were approved by the UC San Diego Institutional Review Board, and all participants provided informed consent before taking part.

The simulation of Fig. 1 used REM (Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997), with items as 49-feature vectors, across 10,000 simulated recognition experiments. In the inversion (N = 50), preregistered face (N = 100) and image set (N = 450) experiments, participants studied lists of images and then made old/new recognition judgments with confidence ratings, and memory was scored as hit rate minus false alarm rate (and as d a in the face experiment). Summed similarity of THINGS concepts was computed from the embedding derived from human similarity judgments (Hebart et al., 2020) and from macaque inferotemporal responses (Papale et al., 2025). Full methods, exclusion criteria and statistical procedures are in SI Appendix, Sections 1, 3, 5 and 8.

Experimental Procedures and Analysis

Statistical Analysis and Exclusion Criteria:

All experiments used within-subjects designs with no randomization of participants to groups required. Consistent with our typical lab practice, data exclusion criteria were (1) Subjects who responded with the same key for more than 80% of trials (response bias), (2) Subjects with more than 20% of trials with reaction times <200 ms (fast responses) or >7,500 ms (slow responses), (3) Subjects with poor overall performance (difference between hits and false alarms < 0.05). After subject exclusion, individual trials with reaction times <200 ms or >10,000 ms were additionally removed from analysis. Notably, corrected recognition (CR) is not an appropriate measure of memory performance in the general case (see Brady et al., 2023). However, it is the measure the memorability literature has historically used, which makes our results more comparable to those of Kramer et al. (2023). In this particular case, because we had a separate study and test period in all of our experiments and 50% of items were old vs. new at test, people's criteria were relatively neutral (criterion c = 0.29 in the image set experiments), thus making this measure relatively unbiased.

Notably, this is unlike the continuous recognition paradigm common in this literature (Berch, 1976; Donaldson & Murdock, 1968; Fox & Osth, 2023; Han & Dobbins, 2008) where the criterion can exceed 0.8. In the continuous recognition paradigm there are generally few false alarms because the default response if you do not hit a key is "new" (you only hit keys for old items) and very few items are actually old (and participants shift their criterion with the base rate of old items; Rhodes & Jacoby, 2007), leading to near-floor false alarm rates that make accurate measurement of memory performance difficult or impossible (Section 2). This also leads to the data being at a point in the ROC where accurate measures like d a and d′ differ most from corrected recognition. By contrast, at the more neutral response criterion people use in our experiment, hits minus false alarms is highly correlated with more accurate measures like d a (r = 0.98, 95% CI [0.97, 0.98], p < 0.01), though because we could not measure the slope of the z-ROC per category, we computed d a with a fixed slope of 0.80 (Didi-Barnea et al., 2016) in this case, which is approximately what is generally found in recognition memory experiments.

Feature Analysis.

For each image set, we extracted the 49 visual and semantic features per concept following Hebart et al. (2020). We computed Spearman correlations between feature values and CR scores across concepts. Bootstrap analysis with 1,000 iterations was conducted, resampling participants within each image set to test the predicted reduction in the sum of the 49 squared correlations from the maintained to the reduced image set (Fig. 2h). The one-sided p is the proportion of resamples in which this sum did not drop. To ask whether the variability of memorability itself was reduced, we estimated the reliability-corrected variance of concept memorability on the 559 concepts tested in both sets: participants were split at random into two halves (200 splits), concept corrected recognition was computed from the pooled trials of each half, and the covariance of the two halves' values across concepts, to which trial-to-trial noise does not contribute, was averaged over splits. The maintained and reduced sets were compared with a permutation test that assigned the 300 participants at random to two groups of 150 (2,000 permutations, 10 splits each), with a two-sided p. For the feature analysis, the drop in each feature's squared Spearman correlation with concept corrected recognition from the maintained to the reduced set was correlated, across the 49 features, with the feature's squared correlation with summed similarity in the maintained set, both directly and as a partial Spearman correlation controlling for the feature's squared correlation with corrected recognition in the maintained set.

Statistical Reporting.

Unless stated otherwise, the confidence intervals reported with each statistic are 95% percentile bootstrap intervals from 10,000 resamples. In our experiments we resampled participants, except for correlations over items or concepts, for which we resampled the items or concepts. In published datasets we resampled concepts or images, and in simulations we resampled simulated items. For paired t tests we report the t-based 95% confidence interval of the mean difference and Cohen's dz . All tests are two-sided except the tests of the predicted reduction in Fig. 2h and Table S1, which are one-sided and reported by their p value alone. For the correlations across the 49 features in Fig. 2 and in the corresponding monkey results, the interval and the p value both come from the bootstrap, resampling concepts (Fig. 2a) or participants (Fig. 2d to g) with the features held fixed, because the 49 features are the full embedding rather than a sample of features. The p value is twice the share of resamples on the far side of zero, and none of the 10,000 resamples crossed zero in any of these tests.

The Image Set Correlations Do Not Depend on the Exclusions

Recomputing without exclusions. The image set experiments excluded participants who did not appear to be doing the task (as described above), which removed 152 of the 602 participants run and left 150 per set. We recomputed the results on all 602, removing no participants or trials (Table S1). Without exclusions, memorability still correlated negatively with summed similarity in all sets (all p < 0.001), and applying the exclusions changed each correlation by at most 0.04, each time making it slightly stronger. The feature-level results of the maintained and changed image sets (Fig. 2d to g) held without exclusions, and a stricter corrected-recognition floor of 0.10 changed none of these correlations by more than 0.02. Thus, the exclusions reduce noise in these estimates but they do not produce the link between distinctiveness and memorability.
