Section 2. Measuring Memory

We report memorability as corrected recognition (hit rate minus false alarm rate) because it is the score the memorability literature uses (e.g., Kramer et al., 2023). We report hits and false alarms separately wherever that is key to our point (Fig. S18). However, we note that corrected recognition is not a good measure of memory in general (Brady et al., 2023). Corrected recognition tracks more accurate signal detection measures only when responding is close to a neutral criterion and false alarms are away from floor (Brady et al., 2023). In this case, we use it because both are true in our image-set experiments, which had separate study and test phases with half of the test items old. Computed from the mean concept hit and false alarm rates of the 450 analyzed participants, the criterion was c = 0.29.

Corrected recognition, d′ and d a.

To examine the extent to which the measure mattered in our study, we scored each concept tested in each image set in three ways: corrected recognition, d′, and d a , the version of d′ that allows old and new items to differ in variability (Macmillan & Creelman, 2004). Because a z-ROC slope cannot be estimated for each concept from a few dozen trials, we computed d a with a slope of 0.80 (Didi-Barnea et al., 2016), a typical value in recognition memory. Corrected recognition and d a ordered concepts almost identically (r = 0.98, 95% CI [0.97, 0.98], p < 0.001, n = 2,453 concept scores; Fig. S2), and corrected recognition agreed nearly as well with d′ (r = 0.96, 95% CI [0.95, 0.96], p < 0.001), showing that the agreement does not depend on the assumed slope. At the slope our six-point confidence ratings give when considered in general (0.59), the correlation was also strong, r = 0.98 (95% CI [0.98, 0.99]).

Thus, at this near-neutral criterion, reporting corrected recognition does not change which items count as memorable.

When false alarms are near floor. The continuous recognition task that produced the THINGS memorability scores is different. Its measure is almost certainly not an accurate measure of memory per se. With a mean false alarm rate of 0.02 across 26,107 images, the published "memorability" score is effectively solely an index of hit rate (r = 0.987, 95% CI [0.987, 0.988]) and not false alarm rate (r = -0.08, 95% CI [-0.09, -0.07]; Fig. S18c).

An effect of similar items in the study list that acts through false alarms is therefore effectively not at all present in the memorability literature, as criteria are so extreme in this task that it is unknown how strong memory actually is for each item (e.g., how many additional hits could people get before they began really false alarming?). A hit rate also cannot separate better memory from a greater willingness to say "old", since an image that makes people more inclined to respond "old" will have more hits whether or not it is better remembered, and with false alarms near floor for all images the score has no way to correct for this (Macmillan & Creelman, 2004). Thus, we strongly believe future memorability studies should use a more standard study-test design or at minimum ensure participants are reliably above floor on false alarm rates.

Section 3. Simulations Across Parameters, Procedures, Representations and Models

The simulations in the main text, and our simulation of Bylinskii et al. (2015) below, run REM at one setting of its parameters, with features drawn from a geometric distribution, in a study-test list procedure. Here we show that their results hold more generally and hold when REM is replaced by a hybrid-similarity exemplar model that computes rarity from the study list rather than from a 'world rarity' as REM relies on.

REM Parameters

Parameter sweep. To test whether the relationship between distinctiveness and memorability depends on the setting used in Fig. 1, we ran 32 simulations that crossed REM's g with the number of features and varied storage probability, copy fidelity, list length and decision criterion one at a time around the standard values of Shiffrin and Steyvers (1997). Distinctive items were more memorable in all 32 (ρ = -0.65 to -0.28, all p < 0.001; Fig. S3a), including at the standard Values"); each group to the right also includes its own rerun of the standard values. (b) The same correlations against overall d′.

Stable Memorability Across Contexts

Context manipulation. The strongest evidence offered for intrinsic memorability is that the rank order of items' memorability is stable across large changes in context. In particular, Bylinskii et al. (2015) measured memorability for the same target scenes in two very different contexts: within-category (e.g., amusement park images studied alongside other amusement parks) and across-category (amusement park images studied alongside houses, pastures, and mountains).

Memorability in the two contexts was similar (Spearman ρ = 0.60 for hit rates), which has been taken to show that memorability reflects properties of the image that are independent of context.

A global matching model with no intrinsic memorability produces the same stability under the same manipulation, because adding many items from the same category makes all of the items in that category harder to remember without causing rank order change in which of them are the most distinctive.

Simulation. We simulated both experimental contexts in REM to test whether this consistency requires intrinsic memorability. We generated 21 categories with 300 items each (75 targets, 225 fillers), matching the structure of Bylinskii et al. (2015). Items were represented as 49feature vectors, with the first 10 features being a proxy for category membership (i.e., being identical for all category members).

Results.

Our REM simulations closely replicated the human findings. Items in Fig. S4a showed consistent memorability across contexts (Spearman ρ = 0.60, 95% CI [0.56, 0.63], p < 0.01), despite REM having no concept of intrinsic memorability and making all memory decisions relationally. The color gradient in Fig. S4a shows that items with lower summed similarity (more distinctive, shown in yellow-green) tended to be more memorable in both contexts, with withincategory memorability correlating with summed similarity in the within-category context (ρ = -0.25, 95% CI [-0.30, -0.20], p < 0.01) and across-category memorability also showing this relationship with its own context (ρ = -0.54, 95% CI [-0.58, -0.51], p < 0.01).

We can see why by examining summed similarity across contexts. Fig. S4b shows that items that were distinct in the across-category context remained distinct within-category (Spearman ρ = 0.93, 95% CI [0.92, 0.94], p < 0.01). Adding category members had a main effect of increasing all items' summed similarity, but preserved the rank order of distinctiveness. This explains how in previous work, highly memorable items like Thomas the Tank Engine maintained their rank order both within the amusement park category and across all other categories (e.g., Bylinskii et al., 2015). It remained an outlier because its distinctive features (a rare combination of animate face features with mechanical features) are uncommon both among other amusement parks and across mixed categories. Adding exemplars from the same amusement park category like ferris wheels and roller coasters shifts Thomas's summed similarity higher but doesn't eliminate its outlier status or affect its rank order with respect to distinctiveness. Since both contexts sample from the same image set, items that are distinct in the full image set tend to remain distinct within their category and with respect to the test lures.

Other criteria and category structures.

In the REM simulation of Bylinskii et al. (2015; Fig. S4a), an item's memorability among members of its own category predicted its memorability among items from other categories. We repeated this simulation 18 times, varying one factor at a time: the decision criteria in the two contexts, the number of category-defining features, the number of categories and the number of items per category. Memorability ranks were consistent across contexts in all simulations (ρ = 0.24 to 0.76, all p < 0.001; Fig. S4c). This also held when both contexts used the same criterion (ρ = 0.24 to 0.54), indicating that the consistency does not come from a difference in criteria between contexts. In all simulations, items distinctive in the whole set stayed distinctive within their category (summed similarity across contexts, r = 0.79 to 1.00). The cross-context consistency of Fig. S4a therefore does not depend on a particular category structure or decision criterion. Simulation details. We generated 21 simulated 'scene categories', each containing 300 items (75 targets and 225 fillers), matching the structure of Bylinskii et al. (2015). Items were represented as arbitrary 49-d feature vectors with all parameters identical to the REM simulation of Fig. 1: features drawn from a geometric distribution (g = 0.65), encoding probability = 0.3, and correct encoding probability = 0.6. To create categorical structure, we designated the first 10 features as category-defining features. For each category, we generated a category prototype by drawing 10 feature values from the geometric distribution. All items within that category shared these 10 category-defining feature values, while the remaining 39 features varied independently across items.

We then simulated two experimental contexts corresponding to Bylinskii et al.'s design.

In the within-category simulation, we conducted separate recognition memory experiments for each of the 21 categories. Consistent with empirical data, we varied the recognition criterion between experiments: within-category simulations used a criterion of 20, while across-category simulations used a criterion of 5 to reflect participants' actual tendencies to adopt a more conservative criterion as items become more similar (e.g., Nosofsky & Kantner, 2006).

For each simulation run, we randomly sampled 30 targets and 90 fillers from within a single category, encoded them following standard REM procedures, and tested recognition memory against a decision criterion of 20. In the across-category simulation, we tested the same target items in mixed-category contexts. For each simulation run, we randomly sampled 30 targets and 90 fillers across all 21 categories and tested recognition memory against a criterion of 5. For the across-category context, we conducted 1,000 simulation runs. For the within-category context, we conducted 1,000 simulation runs per category (21,000 total). This yielded stable memorability estimates (hit rate minus false alarm rate) for each target item. False alarm rates were computed by testing each target's familiarity signal against separately generated novel lures.

Finally, we again computed summed similarity using the same L2 norm approach described in Section 1. Mirroring the structure of the simulated memory experiments, in the within-category simulation each item's summed similarity was computed as the negative of the average

Euclidean distance to all other items within its category. In the across-category simulation, each item's summed similarity was computed as the negative of the average Euclidean distance to all items across all categories.

Continuous Recognition

Adapting REM to continuous recognition. As noted above, memorability has often been measured with continuous recognition rather than with the study-test lists of Fig. 1. Continuous recognition has no separate phases, since each trial tests the item on screen and is also a new study event. We adapted REM to run this task trial by trial while keeping its decision rule.

Memory grows during the session. On each trial the item on screen is compared with all traces stored on earlier trials, using REM's likelihood ratio (Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997), and the model responds "old" when the average likelihood ratio across those traces exceeds its criterion. After the response, the item is stored as a new trace, whether it was shown for the first time or repeated. A repeat is therefore judged against a memory that holds its own earlier trace along with all other items stored so far. Because continuous recognition produces far fewer false alarms than a study-test list, we did not use REM's usual criterion of 1.0 but set it so that the model's false alarm rate matched the participants' rate of 2%. Because traces were never forgotten, any loss of memory over a session comes from interference among the stored traces.

Simulated THINGS trial sequences. Each simulated participant followed the trial sequence of one participant in the original THINGS memorability study in terms of old vs. new items (Kramer et al., 2023), taken from the raw trial-level data, with first showings and repeats in the same order and at the same lags. We used the sequences of 400 participants, with ten simulated participants on each. Because each distinct image was replaced by an item with REM's generated features, the similarity of the preceding items to each probe arose only by chance.

We ran the model at the standard storage probability (0.30) and at a higher one (0.75) that brings its overall d′ close to participants'. As in the data, the same item was remembered less well when the items shown before it were more similar (Fig. S5). In particular, d′ fell by 0.51 in the data and by 0.63 and 1.12 in the model (depending on its parameters; Spearman ρ = -1.00 to -0.98), and false alarms more than doubled in the data and in the standard model and rose tenfold at the higher storage probability (ρ = 0.98 to 1.00). At the higher storage probability the measured criterion also became more liberal with similar preceding items, as in the data (ρ = -1.00; data, ρ = -0.79). Because the model's threshold is fixed, this apparent shift is not a criterion shift per se but reflects a stronger memory signal for new items that resemble recent ones, which, when analyzed post hoc, can falsely appear to be a criterion shift. Thus, a global matching model produces the context cost of the continuous recognition task, and an apparent criterion shift, with no item-intrinsic memorability and no strategic adjustment.

List Context

The same item on crowded and uncrowded lists. Global matching models predict that an item's memorability depends on the items it is studied with, as well as the lures it is tested against. To test this directly in the model, we held each item fixed and changed only the other items on its 40-item study list, at the parameter values of Fig. 1. On random lists, close neighbors appeared by chance. On designed lists, we placed 16 of an item's close neighbors on its list and used its nearest neighbor, never studied, as its lure. Crowded lists raised both hits and false alarms, but raised false alarms more (designed lists: hits +0.08, 95% CI [0.07, 0.09]; false alarms +0.11, 95% CI [0.10, 0.12]). Thus, d′ fell (Fig. S6), by 0.07 (95% CI [0.06, 0.09]) on random lists and by 0.13 (95% CI [0.09, 0.17]) on designed lists. Because both rates rose together, corrected recognition registered little of this cost. In the model, the same item is remembered less well when its list makes it less distinctive. The cost is clearest in d′, which does not depend on the overall rate of "old" responses.

Measured Representations

REM with measured features. In standard REM, an item is a list of features whose values are drawn at random from a geometric distribution. Thus, which items resemble each other is decided by chance. To test whether the crowding effects depend on that generated structure, we made each simulated item a THINGS concept (Hebart et al., 2019), such that its features were the concept's 49 SPoSE values (Hebart et al., 2020), dimensions derived from people's choices of the odd one out among three objects (e.g., how animal-related or food-related a concept is).

Thus, human similarity judgments, rather than the simulation, determined which items were similar and which were distinctive (results in Fig. S7).

Because SPoSE values are continuous rather than discrete like REM's, the model kept REM's likelihood ratio but changed how the rarity of a value is judged and how a probe value is matched to a stored one. The rarity of a feature value was judged against the distribution of that feature across the 1,600 concepts. Thus, agreeing on a value that few concepts share counts for more than agreeing on a common one, as in REM (Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997). Because two continuous values never match exactly, the model adds one parameter, retention noise. A correctly stored feature is set to the studied value plus Gaussian noise, with a standard deviation set as a fraction of that feature's spread across concepts. A probe value then counts as evidence for a trace according to how close it falls to the stored value under that noise, relative to how common the value is among all concepts. The study and test design and the storage and copy parameters were identical to those in Fig. 1, and we report results at several noise levels rather than fitting the noise. We find, as expected, that concepts that sit close to their 20 nearest neighbors were less memorable (ρ = -0.52 to -0.44, all p < 0.001, n = 1,600 concepts; -0.55 with REM's generated features in the run of Fig. 1; Section 4 gives the relationship at every scale), and a concept studied with its 16 closest neighbors lost 0.34 to 0.44 in d′, more than with REM's generated features (0.13), because false alarms to its nearest neighbor rose (Fig. S7). Both signatures of the main-text simulations therefore arise when distinctiveness comes from the measured similarity structure of THINGS concepts.

A Hybrid-Similarity Exemplar Model

The model. REM is one of many global matching models. To test whether our simulation results depend on REM's likelihood ratio and use of world rarity to weight rare features, we replaced it with a hybrid-similarity exemplar model (Knapp et al., 2006; Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003), keeping the generated features, encoding and lists of Fig. 1. In this model, familiarity is the summed similarity of the probe to the stored traces. The similarity of a probe to a trace is exp(-c•d) × exp(γ•m), where d is the Euclidean distance between them over the features the trace stored and m is the number of stored features on which they share a distinctive value. We defined a feature value as distinctive when three or fewer of the 40 items on that simulated participant's own study list had it. Thus, rarity was defined by the study list alone and not by a long-term base rate or world rarity. We used γ = 2 and a fixed criterion at a false alarm rate of 0.15, without fitting either. The similarity width c was set to the value, among nine candidates, that brought overall d′ closest to REM's (c = 1.42 at γ = 2 and 2.26 at γ = 0).

Simulation results. The model reproduced the qualitative pattern of all three simulation results.

Isolated items were more memorable (ρ = -0.32, 95% CI [-0.36, -0.27], compared with -0.61 in REM at the Fig. 1 values, in the run of Fig. S3; Fig. S8a). On designed lists, studying 16 of an item's close neighbors raised its hits by 0.06 (95% CI [0.04, 0.07]) and false alarms to its nearest neighbor by 0.13 (95% CI [0.12, 0.14]), and d′ fell by 0.26 (95% CI [0.22, 0.29], n = 200 critical items; Fig. S8b and c). In the simulation of the Bylinskii et al. (2015) context manipulation, an item's memorability within its category predicted its memorability across categories (ρ = 0.48, 95% CI [0.44, 0.52], n = 1,575 targets; positive in all 19 settings of a sweep over criteria, category structure and model parameters, ρ = 0.15 to 0.74). The effects are not matched in size to REM's, since overall accuracy was lower in this model (d′ of 0.82, and 0.66 in the GCM, compared with 1.61). The advantage for isolated items held in 25 of 26 settings of a parameter sweep (ρ = -0.47 to +0.01) and depended on the weight given to rare matches. With γ = 0, which is the generalized context model (Nosofsky, 1986), not the hybrid version, the listcontext cost remained but isolated items were no longer more memorable (ρ = +0.26, 95% CI [0.22, 0.31]). This suggests that weighting distinctive features more is key to explaining memorability through crowding, although our simulations do not determine the extent to which this weighting must be based on world rarity (as in REM) vs. list rarity (as in the Hybrid-GCM model).

Section 4. A Unified Measure of Distinctiveness Across Analyses

The analyses in the main text and elsewhere in this appendix measure how crowded an item is in several ways, depending on what kind of model is used and what the shape of the data is (e.g., discrete vs. continuous). Here we apply a unified measure to each dataset and vary how local it is (e.g., how much the nearest items contribute vs. all items), reporting hits, false alarms and d′ separately to show robustness and the patterns of hits and false alarms.

Our measure. For each item, we defined crowding as the mean of exp(-d/τ) over the other items, where d is 1 minus the Pearson correlation of two concepts' SPoSE vectors, or the Euclidean distance between two simulated items divided by its median where appropriate.

When τ is small (e.g., τ = 0.05), only an item's nearest neighbors contribute. As τ grows, all items in the set count more equally, and in the limit crowding is the mean similarity to the whole set. Crowding was computed at τ = 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4 and 1 and in the all-items limit, in seven datasets. These were the REM simulation of Fig. 1, the REM model on SPoSE features of Fig. S7, the hybrid model with rarity computed from the study list of Fig. S8, the original THINGS memorability data (concept hit rates on target repeats and false-alarm rates on first showings, computed from the trial records of Kramer et al., 2023), and the maintained, changed and reduced image sets.

Crowding raises false alarms in all datasets and at all scales. Crowded items were falsely recognized more often in all seven datasets at every value of τ (Fig. S9a; Spearman ρ from 0.11 to 0.75), and in the image sets this held within higher-level categories as well (ρ = 0.14 to 0.29 in the maintained and changed sets). Global matching models predict exactly this, because a new item that resembles many studied items produces a strong match to them.

Hits reflect two influences that crowding pulls in opposite directions. In global matching models, a probe that resembles many stored items receives extra matches, which raises both hits and false alarms. Most of these models also weight a match by how rare the matching features are, which raises hits for items with rare features. REM computes that rarity against the observer's lifetime experience (Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997), whereas hybrid-similarity models compute it against the items on the study list (Knapp et al., 2006; Nosofsky & Zaki, 2003).

Thus, whereas false alarms should depend mainly on the first influence (and indeed, they rose with crowding at all scales), hits depend on the balance between the two. When crowding also makes an item's features common, as it does in REM, crowded items draw fewer hits. In the hybrid model at the settings of Fig. S8, the extra matches outweigh the bonus for rare features, and crowded items draw more hits (Fig. S9b). The balance between the two influences therefore decides the direction of the hit effect.

In people the hit effect was small and varied in sign across datasets and scales. When crowding changed for a concept between image sets, its false alarms rose (ρ = 0.14 and 0.45), while its hits stayed the same (ρ = -0.01) or fell (ρ = -0.34), and the same image after a more similar stream drew more false alarms and no more hits (Fig. S15).

Crowding lowers d′ at all scales. Because false alarms rose more than hits, even when hits went up, d′ fell with crowding in all datasets (Fig. S9c), from -0.13 to -0.20 in THINGS, -0.13 to -0.48 in the maintained set, -0.45 to -0.48 in the changed set and -0.04 to -0.17 in the reduced set, compared with -0.17 to -0.63 in the three models.

Corrected recognition can reverse the sign. Because false alarms in the THINGS task are near floor (Section 2) and nearest-neighbor crowding goes with more hits across THINGS concepts, corrected recognition can rise with crowding even though d′ falls. This is a pitfall of the inability to criterion-correct memory from this task. For example, the feature-level analysis of Fig. 2a shows this (Table S2). Measured with d′, features that predict crowding predict poorer memory at all scales, whereas measured with corrected recognition the relationship reverses for the most local measures. The same analysis in the changed set holds at all scales with either measure, and in the maintained set at all scales except the most local one. Crowding measured over each THINGS concept's five nearest concepts in the deep-network spaces of Section 7 shows the same pattern, with more crowded concepts receiving more false alarms (ρ = 0.33), slightly more hits (ρ = 0.07) and lower d′ (ρ = -0.18). Thus, crowding did not predict corrected recognition (ρ = 0.03, p = 0.23).

The reduced set. The reduced set was built to equalize the summed similarity of Fig. 2, and it halved the spread of crowding measured over the whole set (SD ratio, reduced to maintained, 0.51 in the all-items limit). However, it did not equalize crowding by nearest neighbors, whose spread across concepts was similar or larger in the reduced set (SD ratio 1.2 at τ = 0.2 and 2.6 at τ = 0.05), because the selection process was done at the level of concepts. This suggests that the reduction of Fig. 2h is best described as a reduction in how much concepts differ in their similarity to the set as a whole.

Section 5. The Rare-Feature Face Experiment

The inversion experiment changed what each item was studied alongside without changing the test structure. However, global matching models also predict that what an item is tested against should be key to its memorability. Our second experiment tests this prediction with faces, focusing on a version of the tattoo example in the main text. In particular, we held the studied faces fixed and changed only whether a new face at test contained the same rare feature. Participants studied 50 synthetic faces (N = 100, preregistered; Methods below).

Six of the studied faces had a feature that is rare in everyday life: an electric-green mohawk, a long forked beard, and four combinations of makeup, ink, piercings and eyewear. Each of these features was carried by a pair of different people (e.g., two different people with the mohawk).

One member of each pair was studied, chosen at random for each participant, and the other could appear at test as a lure with the same feature.

Our manipulation was therefore at the level of the feature rather than the face. A rare feature appeared at test on the face that had been studied, and on a new face that had not. The rest of the test was ordinary faces, half of them studied and half new. If a rare feature makes a face intrinsically memorable, it should improve memory overall. If memorability is relational relative to the test items, not only the study items, the feature should help only when no new face at test also has it.

We found that studied faces with a rare feature were called old more often than ordinary studied faces (0.90 vs. 0.80, t(99) = 5.29, p < 0.001; Fig. S10b). However, new faces with a rare feature were also called old more often, relative to new faces with no rare feature, and in fact the feature inflated false alarms further than it inflated hits (false alarms 0.59 vs. 0.41, t(99) = 5.89, p < 0.001; increase in false alarms vs. increase in hits, +0.07, 95% CI [0.01, 0.14], t(99) = 2.17, p = 0.033). Thus, consistent with global matching models, matching on a rare feature is strong evidence that a face was studied, but this is true whether or not the rest of the face matches.

Thus, a rare face tested against a new face with the same feature was no more discriminable than an ordinary face (Fig. S10c). Rare faces led to d a = 1.67 (95% CI [1.47, 1.89]) against unrelated new faces and 1.00 (95% CI [0.75, 1.25]) against new faces with their feature, identical to the discriminability of ordinary faces against unrelated new faces (1.00, 95% CI [0.90, 1.11]). Thus, a rare feature made a face more memorable than an ordinary one only if no new face had the same feature, and if new faces shared the same feature, the rare feature actually made faces slightly less memorable than an ordinary face (a drop of 0.18, 95% CI [0.12, 0.24], t(99) = 5.89, p < 0.001, dz = 0.59, and a shortfall of 0.07, 95% CI [0.01, 0.14], t(99) = 2.17, p = 0.033, dz = 0.22; Fig. S12a). Comparing each face against itself across participants, as usual in memorability work, the rare faces were no more memorable than the ordinary ones (hit minus false-alarm rate 0.33 against 0.38; d′ 1.12 against 1.10), since their extra hits (0.90 against 0.79) were matched by extra false alarms (0.57 against 0.41).

Thus, a rare feature does provide a strong match signal, but that is not the same thing as being intrinsically memorable. The feature's effect on memorability depends on the set the face is judged in. It gives a large advantage when no other face has the feature, and loses that advantage as soon as one does. Notably, a global matching model with no term for intrinsic memorability, which we ran through the same design before collecting any data, predicted the direction of each of these preregistered results (Fig. S11). same feature (blue, dashed) gave 1.00 (95% CI [0.75, 1.25]), as did ordinary faces against unrelated new faces (1.00, 95% CI [0.90, 1.11]; dark gray, under the blue line). Black dashed line: chance. Error bars (b): 95% bootstrap confidence intervals over participants.

Methods. This experiment was preregistered (AsPredicted #311640). Stimuli were photorealistic synthetic faces generated with OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra model, each a front-facing studio portrait with a neutral expression on a plain gray background. Twelve faces formed six pairs. The two members of a pair were different people of the same age band, sex and race who had the same rare feature (an electric-green mohawk, a long forked beard, or an unusual combination of makeup, facial ink, piercings or eyewear). The other 59 faces were ordinary faces with none of these features.

Each participant studied 50 faces (one randomly chosen member of each rare-feature pair and 44 ordinary faces) for 3 s each with a 500 ms interstimulus interval, pressing the space bar whenever a face repeated immediately (six ordinary faces that were never tested repeated in this way). After 60 s of arithmetic, they completed 36 old/new recognition trials, each followed by a four-point confidence rating. Three rare-feature pairs were tested with the studied face and three with the unstudied member of the pair, along with 15 studied and 15 unstudied ordinary faces. Memorability (Fig. S12a) was corrected recognition computed for each participant, with the false alarm rate taken either from unstudied ordinary faces or from the unstudied members of the rare-feature pairs, and conditions were compared with paired t-tests. The preregistered signal detection analysis (Fig. S10c) is reported below.

Participants. The final sample was the first 100 participants, recruited online through Prolific, who passed the preregistered exclusion rule (at least 4 of the 6 repeats detected and no more than 5 presses to non-repeated faces during study); 11 additional participants were run and excluded under this rule.

The Model Predicted Each Preregistered Face Result

Predictions made before data collection. We ran REM (Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997) through the face design of Fig. S10 at 729 parameter settings, including its standard values, and preregistered the three predictions it makes (AsPredicted #311640) before running this study: more hits to rare than to ordinary studied faces, more false alarms to a new face with a studied face's rare feature than to a new ordinary face, and a larger advantage for rare faces against unrelated new faces than against same-feature lures. The hit prediction held at 712 of the 729 settings (the exceptions were near ceiling). The false alarm prediction held at all 729, as did the third prediction, computed from the model's evidence (Fig. S11a). After data collection we ran the model again at 243 settings and scored its output the same way we scored the data, with criteria matched to how participants used the rating scale. Rare faces had a higher d a against unrelated new faces than against same-feature lures at 242 of the 243 settings. The rare feature alone raised d a at only 18 (Fig. S11b). Thus, all three predicted differences appeared in the data (hits 0.10, 95% CI [0.07, 0.14]; false alarms 0.18, 95% CI [0.12, 0.23]; lure set 0.67, 95% CI [0.46, 0.92]; all p < 0.001), and the feature itself did not make faces more memorable (0.00, 95% CI [-0.23, 0.24], p = 0.99).

The Preregistered Discriminability Analysis of the Face Study

Rare faces against each kind of lure. The preregistered analysis plan was to measure d a from confidence-based receiver operating characteristics, fitting an unequal-variance signal detection model. The planned sample was the first 100 participants to pass the preregistered exclusion rule. The model was fit to trials pooled over participants with one set of criteria for all kinds of face. The same rare faces gave d a = 1.67 (95% CI [1.47, 1.89]) against unrelated new faces and 1.00 (95% CI [0.75, 1.25]) against their same-feature lures, the value ordinary faces gave against unrelated new faces (1.00, 95% CI [0.90, 1.11]; Fig. S10c). The lure set accounted for the whole advantage. The rare feature alone did not make faces more memorable (Fig. S12b).

Resampling the features.

Because the design has six rare features, we also resampled the features instead of the participants. This widened both intervals but didn't affect the conclusion.

The effect of the lure set still excluded zero (0.67, 95% CI [0.28, 1.23], p < 0.002, the smallest p that 1,000 resamples can resolve) and the effect of the feature itself still included it (0.00, 95% CI [-0.43, 0.42], p = 0.98; Fig. S12b). Leaving out each pair in turn kept the lure-set effect between 0.47 and 0.85, while the feature's own effect stayed near zero and changed sign (-0.12 to 0.15). In hit rate minus false alarm rate (Fig. S12a), rare faces scored 0.49 (95% CI [0.44, 0.55]) when no new face had their feature and 0.32 (95% CI [0.25, 0.39]) when one did, below ordinary faces (0.39, 95% CI [0.35, 0.43]). On neither measure does a rare feature give a face an advantage. Instead, how memorable a face looks depends on what it is tested against.

Section 6. Generality Across Image Sets and Embeddings

The THINGS analyses rest on one image set of objects and on one embedding of 49 features.

Here we test whether the link between distinctiveness and memorability depends on either choice.

Faces and Scenes

Summed similarity in deep-network spaces. We embedded all released images of a face image set (Bainbridge et al., 2013) and a scene image set (Isola et al., 2011), unscored fillers included, in the 14 deep-network spaces of Section 7, and computed each scored image's summed similarity to the whole set, with all features weighted equally or with feature weights fitted on other images of the same image set. All correlations with memorability were computed on held-out images.

We found that more crowded images were remarkably less memorable in both image sets (Fig. S13a; equal weights, faces ρ = -0.47, 95% CI [-0.50, -0.43], scenes ρ = -0.50, 95% CI S13b). Distinctiveness within an image set therefore predicts memorability for faces and scenes as it does for objects, with similarity measured in spaces that contain no human judgments.

Embedding Size

SPoSE refits. The 49 SPoSE features are the ones published by Hebart et al. (2020) and that Kramer et al. (2023) analyzed memorability with respect to, and we used them as published.

SPoSE (Zheng et al., 2019) learns these features directly from people's odd-one-out choices.

Each concept receives a non-negative weight on each candidate feature, and the similarity of two concepts is the overlap of their weights. The weights are adjusted until the model predicts which object people picked as the odd one out in each set of three. A sparsity penalty pushes features the choices do not need toward zero, and features left with no substantial weight on any concept are removed. The number of features is therefore not chosen in advance. It depends on the penalty and on the amount of data (e.g., the larger THINGS-data release yields 66 features; Hebart et al., 2023).

To test whether our results depend on this number, we refit SPoSE from scratch to the raw THINGS-data choices, starting from 100 candidate features, at a range of penalty strengths, then recomputed summed similarity in each refit's own features and repeated the analyses. In all refits in which the penalty removed features, leaving between 6 and 81, the least distinctive features were again the least memorable (r = -0.81 to -0.50 across the 14 refits, p < 0.01 with 17 or more features and p = 0.053 with 6, compared with -0.61, 95% CI [-0.68, -0.51], for the published embedding; Fig. S14), and the four image-set correlations of Fig. 2d to g that use SPoSE features kept their signs.

Section 7. Context Effects in the Original THINGS Data

The trial-level records of the original memorability study with THINGS (Kramer et al., 2023) allow a direct test of context. Because each participant in continuous recognition sees a different stream, the same image appears after preceding images that are sometimes similar to it and sometimes not. Comparing an image with itself across these streams holds everything about the image constant and varies only its context.

The Same Image After Different Streams

Within-image context. For each trial we measured how similar the preceding stream was to the probe (the mean SPoSE similarity of the most similar images already shown) and ranked each image's trials into bins by that similarity, so that all bins hold the same images. Across bins, d′ fell at each step, a decline of 0.51 (95% CI [0.48, 0.54], Spearman ρ = -1.00; Fig. S15a), 1.34 times the standard deviation of d′ across images; hits fell and false alarms more than doubled.

Notably, Bainbridge (2026), analyzing the same trials, found that an image's mean similarity to all preceding images explained little variance in hits once each image's memorability was included. That memorability score is the image's average performance across contexts, and so already includes the average effect of context. Comparing the same image across its own contexts, as here, measures the effect directly without removing the variance from contexts first, and finds a large and reliable effect. Feature similarity and category membership. Feature similarity, more than shared category membership, accounted for this effect. With the image held constant, crowding of the preceding stream in SPoSE predicted false alarms 4.6 times (95% CI [2.8, 12.0]) more strongly than the number of preceding items from the probe's higher-level category entered alongside it. Close competitors are also the most common case in this study. Of first showings after at least 20 preceding items, only 7.8% arrive with no item of the probe's higher-level category already shown, and 62% of a concept's ten nearest SPoSE neighbors belong to its own category, compared with 4% by chance. Most images in the memorability study were therefore judged after items from their own category, the items most likely to be their near neighbors.

Kramer et al.'s Quartile Test

The same trials with two tests of context. Kramer et al. (2023) looked for context effects by splitting participants into quartiles by how many exemplars of a category they had seen, and found that the memorability ranking of the category's images survived the split as well as it survived a random split of participants. We reran this test on the trial-level data in six higherlevel categories and computed the within-image context effect of Fig. S15 in the same participants and images. Their test reproduced their result. The correlation between the top and bottom quartiles' image scores fell inside the range of random splits in five categories (animals, ρ = 0.09, n = 2,229 images, compared with 0.07) and below it for food, and never above it (Fig. S16a).

However, in the same animal images, d′ fell by 0.63 (95% CI [0.54, 0.71]) from the least to the most crowded preceding stream over 20 bins. Over five bins it fell by 0.47 (95% CI [0.43, 0.52]) across all quartiles, by 0.49 (95% CI [0.42, 0.56]) within the top quartile alone and by 0.33 (95% CI [0.23, 0.42]) within the bottom, far more than the 0.10 (95% CI [0.04, 0.17]) by which the two quartiles differed (Fig. S16b).

The two tests agree once their scale is compared, because the Kramer et al. method barely selects on the relevant context effect. The quartile split moves mean crowding by only 4% to 17% of the range the within-image bins span, which predicts a top-minus-bottom difference in animal d′ of -0.096, compared with -0.104 observed (95% CI [-0.17, -0.04]).

As in our simulation of Bylinskii et al. (2015; Fig. S4), the split shifts the competitors of every image in a category at once, lowering memory for all of them without reordering them (Fig. S16). Per-image scores inside a quartile are also too noisy (split-half reliability 0.02 to 0.17) for a ranking test to register a shift of this size.

A Similarity Space Without Human Judgments

Deep-network crowding. Because SPoSE is built from human similarity judgments, the context effect of Fig. S15 could in theory come from those judgments rather than from the images. We therefore measured crowding in 14 deep-network spaces (AlexNet, VGG16, ResNet18, InceptionV3, CORnet-S, DINOv3 and CLIP, each at an early and a late layer), using the embedding pipeline of Brady and Robinson (2026). A logistic regression fitted on half of the 21,137 participant sessions weighted the 70 crowding measures (five similarity falloffs per space, each centered within image), and the effect was scored on the other half (2,320,666 trials). In these held-out sessions, d′ fell at each step from the least to the most crowded fifth of each image's trials, by 0.51, compared with 0.39 (95% CI [0.37, 0.41]) for SPoSE binned the same way (0.51 over the 20 bins of Fig. S15). Because the deep-network weighting was fitted to independent trial outcomes, this comparison shows that the effect is present at a similar size when similarity is measured from image features alone.

Section 8. Modeling the Data in Our Experiments

The main text tests whether memorability is relational in three experiments: the memorability inversion experiment (Fig. 1c), the rare-feature face experiment (Fig. S10; Section 5) and the image set experiments (Fig. 2). Here we run a global matching model through the lists participants studied and locate where similar items change memory.

The Model Predicts Memory From Participants' Own Lists

Model run through the experiments.

We gave the continuous-feature REM of Fig. S7 the same study lists and test trials that each participant received. To make this work at an image level, each THINGS image was described by 49 features taken from computer vision models, rather than SPoSE (which is concept level), by using the late-layer activations of AlexNet, VGG16, ResNet18 and CLIP, combined and reduced to 49 dimensions by principal component analysis. We adjusted only two settings, the noise on stored features and the threshold for responding "old". We chose them to match our participants' overall false alarm rate and to come close to their overall hit rate. No parameters were fit to individual items. Any difference the model shows between items therefore comes only from how similar each item was to the other items on its lists (discounting feature values common in THINGS). Thus, its item-by-item results are predictions. In the memorability inversion experiment (Fig. 1c), the model reproduced the

Same image, different set.

In the image set experiments, 1,023 images were tested in more than one set, allowing us to compare each image with itself. An image was better remembered in the set where its most similar set-mates were least similar, with d′ higher by 0.28 (95% CI [0.24, 0.32], p < 0.001), and the model predicted about a third of that change (0.10, 95% CI [0.09, 0.11]; Fig. S17b), although its criterion did not quite match participants', with its hits slightly rising rather than slightly falling with crowding (Fig. S17c). A model whose only information about an item is its similarity to the other items, with no parameter fitted to any item, therefore reproduces the inversion and predicts the direction of the change in memory for the same image between sets.

Similar Items Change Memory Mainly Through False Alarms

Hits and false alarms in the inversion experiment. A similar item on the study list could lower an item's memorability in two ways: by making the studied item harder to recognize, which lowers hits, or by making the item look studied when it was not, which raises false alarms. In the memorability inversion experiment each critical item was studied by some participants and was an unstudied lure for the others, and thus has both a hit rate and a false alarm rate. As the number of similar items on the study list rose from 0 to 8, false alarms to the critical items rose from 0.05 to 0.57 (item-wise Spearman ρ = 0.72, 95% CI [0.50, 0.85], p < 0.001) and d′ fell (ρ = -0.49, 95% CI [-0.75, -0.17], p < 0.01; Fig. S18a and b). Hits rose less, from 0.72 to 0.85 (ρ = 0.43, 95% CI [0.15, 0.65]). This rise follows from the design, because the items given more similar items were the more memorable ones in THINGS, and so their higher hit rates reflect which items were chosen rather than the manipulation. This suggests that a close competitor on the study list acts mainly by making a new item look old, likely at least in part because participants cannot know in advance of seeing a given lure what criterion to set for a particular image. If participants knew they were in a study where "twins" would be present and they had to discriminate twin A from twin B, for example, they would likely set a much higher criterion than if they did not expect such twins until they appeared at test. In the image set experiments false alarms also contributed most of the same-image change in d′ (0.20, 95% CI [0.17, 0.23], of the 0.28; Fig. S17c). The published THINGS score is nearly insensitive to these false alarms, likely a major reason the role of context has been underestimated (Fig. S18c; Section 2).

Memorability as An Emergent Property: How Representational Structure Creates Apparent Intrinsic Effects

Dyllan D. Simpson, John T. Wixted, Timothy F. Brady Corresponding author: Dyllan D. Simpson. Email: dysimpson@ucsd.edu This PDF file includes: Supplementary text (Sections 1 to 8) Figures S1 to S18 Tables S1 to S2 SI References Appendix Section 1. Methods

Computational Modeling: REM

Items were represented as vectors of 49 features, with each feature value drawn from a geometric distribution (with parameter g = 0.65), resulting in integer values starting from 1.

During encoding, each feature was stored with a probability of 0.3, and if stored, was encoded correctly with a probability of 0.6 (otherwise encoded as a random value drawn from the same geometric distribution). These values differ from the standard values of Shiffrin and Steyvers (1997; 20 features, g = 0.40, and a probability of correct encoding of 0.70). At those standard values the relationship between distinctiveness and memorability was similar (ρ = -0.52, 95% CI [-0.56, -0.49], rather than -0.55). It also held across a wide range of other parameter values (Section 3).

We generated a set of 1,600 simulated items to serve as our simulated image set (the same size as the image sets in our behavioral experiments). To mimic typical memorability experimental conditions, including those in our behavioral experiments, we then conducted 10,000 independently simulated recognition memory experiments. Each simulation studied 40 items. Recognition was then tested on 20 randomly chosen studied items plus 20 additional lures drawn from the 1,600-item set. Across the 10,000 simulations, each item served as both a studied probe and a lure probe in different runs, allowing per-item hit and false-alarm rates to be estimated.

Recognition decisions followed standard REM likelihood ratio procedures. For each test item, familiarity was calculated by comparing the test item against all stored memory traces (global matching) vs. the likelihood of these same features being stored if the item was not seen (defined as the generative distribution of items, the geometric distribution). The overall familiarity signal was then computed as the mean likelihood ratio across all stored traces. Recognition responses were determined by comparing this familiarity signal to a fixed criterion of 1.0. For each item across all simulation runs, we calculated hit rate (proportion of correct "old" responses when studied) and false alarm rate (proportion of incorrect "old" responses when unstudied), with memorability operationalized as corrected recognition (hit rate minus false alarm rate).

For each item, we also approximated its distinctiveness in the feature space by computing an approximation of the summed similarity of it to all other items. We did this by calculating the average Euclidean distance to all other items in the image set in the 49-d feature space. Euclidean distance between two items was computed as the L2 norm of the difference between their feature vectors. This measure quantified each item's distance from other items, with larger values indicating greater distinctiveness (Fig. 1 uses the inverse of distance as summed similarity, so that larger values there mean more crowded). Note that unlike the model, this distance metric does not take into account that some features are more rare and thus more informative, nor does it take into account that only items with many overlapping features (not just a few) will give rise to confusable memory signals. It therefore provides only an approximation of the decision rule of the model, but one that can be easily applied to other realistic items in realistic feature spaces.

Behavioral Validation Experiments

Inversion Experiment. For each of the 8 study/test blocks, five critical items were selected from the THINGS image set spanning different memorability levels based on Kramer et al. (2023) scores: one item each from the lowest 20%, 20-40%, 40-60%, 60-80%, and highest 20% memorability bins, giving 40 total items stratified across these memorability bins.

We systematically manipulated each critical item's distinctiveness by varying the number of similar context items in study lists, with the number assigned based on each critical item's original memorability bin: 8 similar items for the top 20% (most memorable), 4 for the 60-80% bin, 2 for the 40-60% bin, 1 for the 20-40% bin, and 0 for the bottom 20% (least memorable).

Because we needed item-wise similarity metrics to select these (which are not available for THINGS from any source based on human judgments), item similarity was computed using representational dissimilarity matrices derived from an average across the 4 RDMs derived from ResNet18, VGG16, AlexNet and CLIP, in each case using the highest layer before the output layer. Each study list contained 40 images: 35 controlled context items (15 similar items distributed across the 5 critical items as described above, plus 20 additional dissimilar exemplars), and 5 additional items selected from the critical items and maximally dissimilar fillers to maintain consistent list length.

Participants performed 8 blocks of study and test. Participants were told to memorize the images for a later memory test. Each studied image was shown for 500 ms with an 800 ms interstimulus interval. In each block participants studied a sequential stream of 40 images, then completed 10 consecutive recognition trials (testing all 5 critical items and all 5 maximally dissimilar items, with old/new status determined by whether each item had appeared in the study stream) judging whether each image was 'old' or 'new' using a 6-point confidence scale.

Whether each tested item was old or new was varied across participants, so that each critical item served as both a studied item and a lure across the sample. Memorability for each critical item was calculated as corrected recognition, then compared to original Kramer et al. (2023) rankings to assess ranking inversion.

Representational Similarity Analysis

We constructed representational dissimilarity matrices (RDMs) over all THINGS concepts for humans (Hebart et al., 2020) and monkeys (Papale et al., 2025). Note that these are at the concept level (effectively categories; e.g., all "keys" or "straws"), not per image.

We derived a behavioral similarity RDM from the large-scale THINGS similarity dataset (Hebart et al., 2020). This dataset provides human behavioral judgments summarized as 49-dimensional SPoSE embeddings for each of the 1,854 object concepts. We treated each embedding as a feature vector and computed pairwise dissimilarities using 1 -Pearson correlation, yielding a symmetric 1,854 × 1,854 RDM. Concept-level memorability values were then attached by aligning each concept to Kramer et al.'s memorability scores. In parallel, we constructed an RDM from the THINGS Ventral Stream Spiking Dataset (Papale et al., 2025). For each concept, multi-unit spiking responses from macaque IT were reduced to a 49-dimensional feature space using principal component analysis to make them comparable to the SPoSE embeddings. These 49 components captured nearly all (85%) of the variance in these responses. As in the human case, we then computed pairwise dissimilarities as 1 -Pearson correlation, yielding a concept-level RDM structurally matched to the human space.

Concept-Weighted Similarity.

For both human and monkey spaces, we derived a categoryweighted dissimilarity measure for each concept. To do this, we took the dissimilarity of each concept to all others in the RDM. These dissimilarities were then weighted by the relative prevalence of each comparison concept's category (i.e., concepts that contained more exemplars contributed proportionally more, to match the memory experiments where generally items are chosen randomly without respect to the concept they belong to). Because we would not expect items that overlap very little to have much impact on the memory of an item, and would expect a disproportionate amount of interference to arise from very similar items (in line with nearly all global matching models of memory: Nosofsky, 1991; Shiffrin & Steyvers, 1997; and other work on how representational distance relates to memory confusability: e.g., Nosofsky, 1992; Schurgin et al., 2020; Shepard, 1987), we used a previously used Gaussian transformation of distance to similarity (Nosofsky, 1992). In particular, the weighted dissimilarities were transformed using a Gaussian kernel centered at minimum dissimilarity (mean = 0, SD = 2) and, because the dissimilarities run only from 0 to 2, this kernel weights all concepts nearly equally, so the measure indexes how close a concept is to the image set as a whole rather than to its nearest neighbors (Section 4 applies one crowding measure, varied from nearest neighbors to the whole set, to every image set in the paper). This produced a single weighted similarity score for each concept, which we use throughout the paper to relate representational structure to memorability.

Image Set Structure Manipulations

Maintained Image Set. The maintained image set was designed to preserve the original THINGS image set structure by maintaining natural feature-similarity relationships. For each concept, we calculated a representativeness score based on how well it matched the original correlation pattern between features and similarity. The representativeness score for each concept was the sum across all of the feature values multiplied by the sign of that feature's correlation with similarity, weighted by the squared magnitude of the correlation. These scores were normalized to create a probability distribution, and 1,600 concepts were sampled with replacement based on these probabilities, ensuring the image set preserved the original representational structure. If a concept was sampled more than once, a distinct image from that concept was added to the image set.

Changed Image Set.

The changed image set systematically inverted which regions of the fixed feature space were densely sampled through a two-stage process. We first identified features positively and negatively correlated with memorability in the original image set. We then computed concept scores by subtracting weighted positive feature values and adding weighted negative feature values (weighted by squared correlation coefficients). From the top 500 scoring concepts (those high on "non-memorable" features), we selected 160 concepts using a greedy algorithm that maximized dissimilarity by starting with the highest scoring concept and iteratively adding concepts with minimum average similarity to already selected items. This created a sparse sampling of typically non-memorable concepts. We then selected 1,440 additional concepts from those scoring high on positive memorability features, sampled with probability proportional to their squared positive scores. This oversampling of typically memorable concepts combined with sparse sampling of typically non-memorable concepts changed the distribution of concepts across the feature space in the direction of inverting the feature relationships to memorability.

Reduced Image Set Construction.

The reduced image set was constructed to reduce correlations between image features and weighted similarity across concepts using an optimization procedure. We tested 500 different exponential transformations of memorabilitypredicting feature scores with exponents ranging from 0.01 to 0.5 (in 0.01 increments, replicated 10 times each). For each transformation, concept scores were normalized from 0 to 1, raised to the test exponent, and used as sampling probabilities for selecting 1,600 concepts with replacement. For each candidate image set, we computed Spearman correlations between all 49 feature dimensions and weighted similarity values (computed as above). The composite score was calculated as the sum of the mean of the correlations and the maximum correlation.

The final image set was selected based on the lowest composite score.

Image Set Structure. Fig. S1 shows the concepts of the reduced image set projected onto the first three principal components of the 49-dimensional feature space (Fig. 2b and c show the maintained and changed image sets).

measures are inherently noisy, limiting the upper bound of what could be explained by an emergent account in these data. In particular, human ratings reflect entire categories (what Hebart et al. call 'concepts') rather than specific images, meaning in those ratings we lack good estimates of within-concept variability. Similarly, monkeys are not humans and monkey visual processing regions capture only one component of the full representational space underlying memory. Nonetheless, these representational spaces can provide complementary tools for examining how distinctiveness within representational space shapes what we remember.

The final sample consisted of 50 participants recruited from UC San Diego who took part in this study in exchange for course credit. Four additional participants were run and excluded based on the above criteria.Image Set Structure Experiments. The final sample consisted of 450 participants across the three image sets: 150 participants in the maintained image set, 150 participants in the changed image set, and 150 participants in the reduced image set, all of whom were recruited from UC San Diego and took part in this study in exchange for course credit. Across all 3 stimulus set experiments, 152 additional participants were excluded based on the above criteria.Experiments were run online and completed on participants' personal devices.Recognition Memory Task. All 3 image set experiments used identical recognition memory procedures. Each participant completed 16 study/test blocks. In each block, they viewed a study list of 40 images, then completed 40 recognition test trials (20 old, 20 new) judging each as 'old' or 'new' on a 6-point confidence scale. Participants were told to memorize the images for a later memory test. Each studied image was shown for 1,000 ms with an 800 ms interstimulus interval.The 20 old items were a subset of the 40 studied images. The 20 new items were drawn at random from the same image set as the studied images. Thus, both the studied items and the lures were random samples of the image set, as in standard memorability studies. Corrected recognition (CR), calculated as hit rate minus false alarm rate, served as the primary memory measure across all experiments.

(a, b) The 40 critical items of the memorability inversion experiment (Fig 1c), each studied alongside 0, 1, 2, 4 or 8 similar items and each studied by some participants and an unstudied lure for the others. (a) Hit rate (blue) and false alarm rate (red), each point the mean over the 8 critical items with the same number of similar items (x-axis), offset horizontally. (b) Mean d′ of the same items. Error bars (a, b): 95% bootstrap confidence intervals across items. (c) Original THINGS data (26,107 images): the correlation across images between the memorability score (hit rate minus false alarm rate, computed from the original trial records) and the hit rate (blue) or the false alarm rate (red). Dashed line: zero.
